explanations.explanation: Other way around, friend. Jehoahaz, king of Israel, kept right on following the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, an earlier king. The verse says plainly, “…he did not turn away from them.” (2 Kings 13:2) That's a man who promises himself one more minute of sleep and then hits snooze six times.

That's it. Jehoahaz did evil in the sight of the LORD, and the verse says, “…he did not turn away from them.” (2 Kings 13:2) The sins came from Jeroboam son of Nebat, an earlier king, and Jehoahaz kept walking right in them. No exit taken, not one.

explanations.answer: He seeks the favor of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The verse says, “Then Jehoahaz sought the favor of the LORD…” (2 Kings 13:4). Aram's king Hazael had been crushing Israel, and Jehoahaz, king of Israel, took it to the LORD. That's the right place to take it.

explanations.answer: He sends gold to King Hazael
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions any gold going to Hazael, king of Aram. What it says is that Jehoahaz, king of Israel, “sought the favor of the LORD” (2 Kings 13:4). Gold in an envelope is the kind of fix that makes you feel clever for about ten minutes. Going to the LORD is the move the verse gives us.

explanations.answer: He asks Egypt to send help
explanations.explanation: Egypt doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. Jehoahaz, king of Israel, did something else: he “sought the favor of the LORD” (2 Kings 13:4). Nobody got put on hold with a faraway country. He went straight to the LORD.

explanations.answer: He saw how Aram oppressed Israel
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says the LORD listened to Jehoahaz, king of Israel, “…because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram had inflicted on Israel.” (2 Kings 13:4) Notice the word saw. The LORD wasn't looking the other way.

No sacrifice is mentioned in this verse. It says Jehoahaz, king of Israel, sought the LORD's favor, and the LORD listened “…because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram had inflicted on Israel.” (2 Kings 13:4) The reason the text gives is what the LORD saw. I'd stick to the reason the verse gives.

The verse doesn't mention any prophets begging. It says the LORD listened to Jehoahaz, king of Israel, “…because He saw the oppression that the king of Aram had inflicted on Israel.” (2 Kings 13:4) The reason is right there in the verse, friend. I'm not adding a crowd of prophets it never put there.

Yes, baker! The text says, “So the LORD gave Israel a deliverer, and they escaped the power of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 13:5) It doesn't name who the deliverer is. It just tells us the LORD gave one and Israel got out from under Aram.

No fortress in this verse. The LORD gave Israel a deliverer, and “they escaped the power of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 13:5) A deliverer is a person who gets you out. A fortress is a thing you hide behind, and this verse is about getting out.

Good word, wrong spot. A covenant does come up later in this passage, in 2 Kings 13:23, but verse 5 says, “So the LORD gave Israel a deliverer…” That's the word that fits this blank. Hang on to covenant, though, because it's coming.

Not this time, friend. The verse starts with “Nevertheless,” and goes on, “…they did not turn away from the sins that the house of Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit, but they continued to walk in them.” (2 Kings 13:6) They were rescued, and they kept walking in the same sins. Rescue came, and the habits stayed.

That's it. After the rescue, “they did not turn away from the sins that the house of Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit, but they continued to walk in them.” (2 Kings 13:6) The Asherah pole even stayed standing in Samaria. Free from Aram, and still walking in the same sins.

Yes, baker. The text says Jehoahaz “had no army left, except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers” (2 Kings 13:7). Ten chariots, and that's all that was left. The king of Aram had destroyed the rest.

It's true, friend, and the number is small. The text says Jehoahaz “had no army left, except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers” (2 Kings 13:7). Ten chariots is all that was left to him. The king of Aram had destroyed the rest.
Right, baker! “And Jehoahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria.” (2 Kings 13:9) Samaria was the capital of Israel, where he had reigned. That's where he was laid to rest too.

Close on the map, but no. Jerusalem is the city of the kings of Judah, and Jehoahaz was king of Israel. The text says, “And Jehoahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria.” (2 Kings 13:9) Samaria is where he reigned, and it's where he was buried.

Bethel isn't mentioned in this verse. It says plainly, “And Jehoahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in Samaria.” (2 Kings 13:9) Samaria is where he reigned over Israel. It's also where he was laid to rest.
Yes, baker! “And his son Jehoash reigned in his place.” (2 Kings 13:9) The crown passed from Jehoahaz to his son. Keep the names straight, because Jehoash and Joash are two different kings.

Ben-hadad is the son of Hazael, king of Aram, and he's on the other side. The text says Jehoahaz's own son took over: “And his son Jehoash reigned in his place.” (2 Kings 13:9) Ben-hadad reigns, but he reigns over Aram, and that comes later in this passage. Different crown, different country.

Amaziah shows up in this passage, but as the king of Judah that Jehoash goes to war against (2 Kings 13:12). He isn't the one who takes Israel's throne. The text says, “And his son Jehoash reigned in his place.” (2 Kings 13:9) That means Jehoahaz's son, in Israel.

You got it, baker. Jehoash “did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit, but he walked in them.” (2 Kings 13:11) A new king, but the same old road. Same road as his father.

explanations.answer: He tears down the Asherah pole
explanations.explanation: No tearing down here. The text says Jehoash “did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit, but he walked in them.” (2 Kings 13:11) The Asherah pole is mentioned back in verse 6, standing in Samaria. Nobody swings a hammer at it in this passage.

explanations.answer: He leads Israel back to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That would've been a nice turn, but it isn't what the text says. Jehoash “did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit, but he walked in them.” (2 Kings 13:11) A new king didn't mean a new start.
Yes, baker. Jehoash, king of Israel, “came down to him and wept over him…” (2 Kings 13:14). Elisha was the prophet, and he was sick with the illness he would die from. The king stood there and wept.

explanations.answer: He asks Elisha to anoint him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about anointing. Jehoash, king of Israel, “came down to him and wept over him…” (2 Kings 13:14). The king came to Elisha, the dying prophet, and he wept.

explanations.answer: He sits beside Elisha in silence
explanations.explanation: Not quiet at all, friend. The king “wept over him, saying, ‘My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!’” (2 Kings 13:14) He cried out. Elisha was a sick prophet, and the king was crying over him.

That's it. “So the king put his hand on the bow, and Elisha put his hands on the king’s hands.” (2 Kings 13:16) The prophet's hands were on the king's hands. I've steadied a wobbly cutter with my mustache before, so I know how that goes.

He did, friend. The text says, “So the king put his hand on the bow, and Elisha put his hands on the king’s hands.” (2 Kings 13:16) Elisha's hands were on top of the king's hands as he held the bow. It's a hands-on lesson, literally.
Yes, baker! Elisha declared, “This is the LORD’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram…” (2 Kings 13:17). He says victory twice, so he means it. That arrow is aimed at Aram.

Peace is a fine word, but Elisha doesn't use it here. He says, “This is the LORD’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram…” (2 Kings 13:17). He says the word victory twice. And it's victory over Aram.

The king had been weeping, so I see why you'd go there. But Elisha says something else: “This is the LORD’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram…” (2 Kings 13:17). The word is victory, said twice. This arrow is good news.

explanations.answer: Until he has put an end to them
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Elisha says, “…you shall strike the Arameans in Aphek until you have put an end to them.” (2 Kings 13:17) That's a full finish, not a partial one. It's a big promise.
Tribute isn't mentioned. Elisha says, “…you shall strike the Arameans in Aphek until you have put an end to them.” (2 Kings 13:17) That's more than getting paid. It's a complete end.

explanations.answer: Until their king asks for peace
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about their king asking for peace. Elisha says, “…you shall strike the Arameans in Aphek until you have put an end to them.” (2 Kings 13:17) The promise is an end, all the way.

explanations.answer: He is angry with the king
explanations.explanation: You got it. “But the man of God was angry with him and said, ‘You should have struck the ground five or six times.’” (2 Kings 13:19) The king struck three times and stopped. Elisha, the man of God, was not happy about it.
No blessing here, friend. “But the man of God was angry with him…” (2 Kings 13:19). Elisha told the king he should have struck five or six times.

No praise came out of that room. The text says, “But the man of God was angry with him…” (2 Kings 13:19). Elisha said the king should have struck the ground five or six times. Three didn't get a pat on the back.

Not quite, baker. Elisha says, “But now you will strike down Aram only three times.” (2 Kings 13:19) Five or six strikes would have ended Aram, but three won't. The word only is doing real work in that sentence.

That's right. Elisha said that five or six strikes would have put an end to Aram, and then he said, “But now you will strike down Aram only three times.” (2 Kings 13:19) Three wins, not a finish. The king stopped, and the promise stopped with him.

Yes, baker. “…they threw the man’s body into Elisha’s tomb.” (2 Kings 13:21) The Israelites saw the raiders and had to move fast. Elisha had died and been buried, and that's where the man's body landed.
No well in this story. The text says, “…they threw the man’s body into Elisha’s tomb.” (2 Kings 13:21) Raiders were coming, and the Israelites did it in a hurry. Elisha's tomb is the place.

A storehouse is a place for storing things, and the text goes somewhere else. “…they threw the man’s body into Elisha’s tomb.” (2 Kings 13:21) With raiders showing up, they didn't have time to do much else. The tomb is where it ended up.

True, friend, and it's one of the wildest verses around. “And as soon as his body touched the bones of Elisha, the man was revived and stood up on his feet.” (2 Kings 13:21) Nobody in that burial party expected that. I think they ran twice as fast as the raiders.

It really is in the text, friend. “And as soon as his body touched the bones of Elisha, the man was revived and stood up on his feet.” (2 Kings 13:21) The man who was thrown in there stood up. Go read it again if you want to be sure.

explanations.answer: His covenant with Israel's forefathers Abraham and Isaac and Jacob
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The text says the LORD “…turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” (2 Kings 13:23) The reason is the LORD's covenant. It isn't anything Israel did.

explanations.answer: The sacrifices Israel's people brought to the altar at Bethel
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about sacrifices at Bethel. It says the LORD “…turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” (2 Kings 13:23) The reason is the covenant. It's not about what the people brought.

explanations.answer: The promise Israel's people made to turn from Jeroboam's sins
explanations.explanation: No such promise appears here. Back in verse 6 we saw that the people “continued to walk in them,” in the sins of the house of Jeroboam. The reason in this verse is that the LORD “…turned toward them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” (2 Kings 13:23)

explanations.answer: The cities Hazael took from Jehoahaz
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. “Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities that Hazael had taken in battle from his father Jehoahaz.” (2 Kings 13:25) Jehoash got back what his father had lost. He won three times, and the cities of Israel came home.

explanations.answer: The gold Hazael took from Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: No gold in this verse. The text says Jehoash “took back from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities that Hazael had taken in battle from his father Jehoahaz.” (2 Kings 13:25) What came back were cities, and they were Israel's.

explanations.answer: The chariots Hazael took from Samaria
explanations.explanation: Chariots aren't mentioned in this verse. It says Jehoash “took back from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities that Hazael had taken in battle from his father Jehoahaz.” (2 Kings 13:25) Cities are what Jehoash took back. He won three times, and the cities of Israel were his again.
